interventions.name: Jali Screen
interventions.description: Decorative lattice screen mounted on south/west/east facades to block direct solar radiation while allowing ventilation.

effect.notes: Typical terracotta jali reduces solar heat gain coefficient by ~45%

citations: Desai & Riddington (2018): Traditional Indian architecture passive cooling strategies
ECBC 2017: Fenestration properties & shading devices

interventions.name: Chhajja (Deep Overhang)
interventions.heritage: Haveli and Jaipur City architecture, Hindu temples
interventions.description: 600–1200 mm horizontal overhang above windows and south/west walls to block high-angle summer sun while allowing winter sun.

effect.notes: Overhang projects solar gains: 600mm depth blocks ~65% summer sun on vertical walls

citations: Olgyay & Olgyay (1957): Design with Climate – passive solar design principles
NBC 2016 Part 11: Overhang sizing for latitude 28.5°N (Delhi)

interventions.name: Aangan (Courtyard)
interventions.heritage: Traditional haveli courtyards, Rajasthan, Gujarat, North India
interventions.description: Central open courtyard (4×4 m to 6×6 m typical) with high walls (~8–10 m) that creates thermal mass, stack effect ventilation, and evaporative cooling.

cost.source: Estimated: structural refurbishment + finishes (retrofit) or integration (new build)

effect.notes: 6×6m aangan, 3m high walls, stack ventilation ~2 ACH; thermal mass time-lag ~2–3 hours

citations: Baker & Steemers (2000): Energy and Environment in Architecture – courtyard cooling
Fathy et al. (1986): Natural Energy and Vernacular Architecture – Middle East/Indian courtyards
Mukerji & Asnani (2016): Adaptive strategies in Indian courtyard houses

interventions.name: Cool Roof (Lime Whitewash)
interventions.heritage: Traditional lime plaster, centuries-old practice across India
interventions.description: High-albedo white lime or acrylic coating on roof to reflect solar radiation and reduce roof surface temperature.

cost.source: CPWD DSR Delhi 2024 (lime or cool-paint application + priming)

effect.notes: Reflects 65–75% of incident solar radiation; reduces roof surface temp by ~20–25°C vs. black surface

citations: Synnefa et al. (2005): A study of the radiative properties of cool coatings
Konopacki & Akbari (2001): Energy savings of cool roofs in US
ECO-Niwas Samhita 2018: Cool roof specs for India (albedo ≥0.65)

interventions.name: Green Roof (Planted Terrace)
interventions.heritage: Terraced gardens, Mughal gardens (Bagh design), modern sustainability
interventions.description: Shallow-depth planted roof (100–150 mm growing medium) with drought-resistant plants, providing evaporative cooling, insulation, and thermal mass.

cost.source: CPWD DSR Delhi 2024 (green roof assembly: substrate, plants, drainage, waterproofing)

effect.notes: Reduces roof heat gain by ~50–70%; evaporative cooling in monsoon adds ~2–3°C reduction

citations: Getter et al. (2007): Carbon sequestration potential of green roofs and living walls
Castleton et al. (2010): Green roofs; building energy savings and the potential for retrofit
ECO-Niwas 2018: Vegetation impact on roof U-value

interventions.name: Rat-Trap Cavity Wall (Rat-Trap Bond)
interventions.heritage: Laurie Baker's modern vernacular innovation (1960s–80s), inspired by traditional Keralan construction
interventions.description: Masonry cavity wall (brick laid in rotated pattern) that creates continuous air voids within the wall body for insulation without added material.

cost.source: CPWD DSR Delhi 2024 (rat-trap bond brickwork labor+material vs. conventional solid wall)

effect.notes: Reduces wall U-value by ~43%; simple labor-intensive technique, no added insulation cost

citations: Laurie Baker (1984): The ecology of building
Raju et al. (2009): Thermal performance of rat-trap bond brickwork
ECO-Niwas 2018: Low-cost thermal mass strategies

interventions.name: Terracotta Cladding + Jali
interventions.heritage: Mughal tile work, temple ornamentation, handmade pottery traditions
interventions.description: Exterior terracotta or clay tile screen (50 mm air gap) on south/west walls provides shading, thermal mass, and evaporative cooling in monsoon.

cost.source: CPWD DSR Delhi 2024 (handmade terracotta tiles + framework + air gap installation)

effect.notes: 40% SHGC reduction + 50mm air gap provides R ~0.2 m²K/W additional resistance

citations: Dornelles & Roriz (2009): Apparent thermal properties of clay brick walls
Traditional Indian architecture: terracotta tile work in hot climates

interventions.name: Khus-Khus Chik (Grass Screen)
interventions.heritage: Ancient cooling technique, used across hot-dry India (Rajasthan, Gujarat)
interventions.description: Vertical screen of dried grass (khus/vetiver root) hung on windows or facades. Water drips from top; evaporation cools incoming air, especially effective in dry season.

cost.source: CPWD DSR Delhi 2024 (simple bamboo frame + khus material, seasonal replacement)

effect.seasonal_notes: Most effective April–June (dry pre-monsoon); impact drops in monsoon
effect.notes: Can cool incoming air by ~5–8°C in dry conditions; requires daily water supply

citations: Bansal et al. (2005): Evaporative cooling for worldwide climatic conditions
Fathy (1986): Natural Energy and Vernacular Architecture – regional cooling techniques

interventions.name: Jharokha (Ventilation Window)
interventions.heritage: Rajasthani haveli jharokhas, Hawa Mahal Jaipur, royal residences
interventions.description: Projecting window/balcony with latticed openings that allows cross-ventilation, reduces glare, and provides shading while controlling direct sunlight.

cost.source: CPWD DSR Delhi 2024 (wooden jharokha fabrication, installation per unit ~1.2m × 1.2m)

effect.notes: Improves cross-ventilation coefficient; moderate solar reduction due to lattice

citations: Riparbelli et al. (2014): Vernacular architecture and passive ventilation in India
Hawa Mahal case study: ventilation efficiency of jharokha design

interventions.name: Clerestory/Ventilator Tower (Badgir-style)
interventions.heritage: Badgirs of Iran/Afghanistan, modified for Indian courtyard architecture
interventions.description: High ventilator or small tower above roof that creates stack-effect ventilation (hot air rises and exits), drawing cool air up through the building.

cost.source: CPWD DSR Delhi 2024 (RCC/brick ventilator construction, typical height 1.5–2m above roof)

effect.notes: Works best with aangan or internal courtyard; ~3 ACH during hot hours

citations: Allard & Ghiaus (2005): Natural ventilation in buildings – stack effect
Badgir design: thermal buoyancy ventilation in hot climates
